content:
With the launch of the all-new iPhone Duo, Apple has made a significant gamble on the software side. All apps will need to be recompiled to at least iOS 27.0 to take advantage of the iPhone Duo's larger internal display. To use Duo's unique new tab bar and other interface elements, an upgrade to iOS 27.1 will be required.

Of course, this means a large number of developers will need to rebuild their apps to support Duo. But on the other hand, Apple is taking a gamble too: many apps on the iPhone Duo may end up stuck in a letterboxed display mode.

An obvious solution would be for Apple to allow resizable iPad apps to run on the iPhone Duo. The cost is that the user experience might feel a bit rough around the edges. With a compatibility layer in place, many developers may also take much longer to support the iPhone Duo's interface elements.

I understand why Apple isn't doing this, because the interface they've designed for the iPhone Duo does feel intuitive and polished. If Apple supported resizable iPad apps, the entire device would end up feeling not much different from a typical Android foldable.

That said, you can't help but wonder how long it will take and how many developers will need to put in the effort just to compile for iOS 27. Compiling for iOS 27 isn't just about supporting Duo—it also means you'll no longer have the option to disable Liquid Glass. For developers who aren't prepared, the latter will give many of them pause about updating to support iPhone Duo.

Given that Duo supports split-screen, as long as Apple allows non-native apps to use split-screen, apps that fail to fully expand on the internal screen may not pose too much of a problem.

However, for mobile games—and I'm sure this will be hugely popular on the iPhone Duo's internal screen—the lack of a true full-screen experience will put off quite a few users.

I really hope Apple's efforts to encourage developers to support the Duo interface will pay off, but I'm genuinely concerned about this. Obviously, only time will tell.

In the worst case, Apple could simply add an iPad app compatibility mode for iPhone Duo in iOS 28, which would both improve the user experience and ensure support for first-wave apps.

I'm really looking forward to the iPhone Duo, but Apple's gamble of requiring developers to support both Liquid Glass and Duo may make the first few months a rather bumpy experience.

Would you buy the iPhone Duo? What are you most looking forward to? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
